Every EdgeCase graph keeps a record of what has been done to it. Each call that builds, changes,
analyzes, or traverses the graph appends a *step* to the graph's *step log*, with the method that
was called, a snippet of code that shows the call, a short narration, and a list of the nodes and
edges it affected. Recording is always on and needs no setup.

The log serves three purposes. It is an audit trail, which answers the question of how a graph came
to be the way it is. It can be exported as a table, to document a data-preparation pipeline next to
its results. And it can be replayed as an animation with `play()`, which shows the graph growing
and changing one step at a time, together with the code behind each step. This makes the log a tool
for teaching graph algorithms, for explaining an analysis to others, and for checking that a
sequence of edits did what was intended.

## Reading the log

A small book club makes a good example. Four friends start the club, two colleagues join at the
second meeting, and one member leaves. `note()` attaches a narration of our own to the next step,
which explains the reason for a step rather than its mechanics:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

club = (
    ec.Graph()
    .note("Four friends start a book club.")
    .add_nodes(["Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee"])
    .add_edges([("Ana", "Ben"), ("Ben", "Cy"), ("Cy", "Dee"), ("Dee", "Ana")])
    .note("At the second meeting, Cy brings two colleagues, Eve and Fay.")
    .add_nodes(["Eve", "Fay"])
    .add_edges([("Cy", "Eve"), ("Cy", "Fay"), ("Eve", "Fay")])
    .note("Ben moves away and leaves the club.")
    .delete_node("Ben")
)
club.degree_centrality()
club.bfs(start="Ana")
club.count_nodes(), club.count_edges()
```

The club ends with five members and five friendships. The `steps` property returns the log. It
prints as a numbered list with the kind of each step and the method that made it:

```{python}
club.steps
```

There are seven steps, one for each call that changed or analyzed the graph. The breadth-first
search is a single step with five *sub-steps*, one for each node it visited. Read-only calls, such
as the `count_nodes()` and `count_edges()` above, `get_node_df()`, or `neighbors()`, are not
recorded, so the log stays focused on the operations that matter. `print_steps()` prints the same
summary without the list brackets, which suits scripts and logs:

```{python}
club.print_steps()
```

### Steps in detail

The log is a `StepList`, a Python list with a few extra methods, and each of its entries is a `Step`
object. A step's `code` shows the call that made it, written with `G` standing for the graph, and
its `narration` describes it in words. The narration comes from `note()` when one was given, and is
generated automatically otherwise:

```{python}
[(step.code, step.narration) for step in club.steps[:2]]
```

The second step had no note, so EdgeCase described it as four edges that connect four nodes.
Long arguments, such as the dictionary of values passed to `set_node_attrs()`, are abbreviated in
the code, so the snippets are a readable record rather than a script to run.

Each step also has a `delta`, which lists exactly what the step changed. Nodes and edges are given
by their labels, or by their IDs when they have no label:

```{python}
removal = club.steps[4]
removal.delta.nodes_removed, removal.narration
```

The delta has fields for added, removed, and modified nodes and edges, for the attributes that were
changed, for the nodes and edges a selection picked out, and for the scores and groups computed by
an analysis. For the degree centrality step, the scores themselves are kept:

```{python}
club.steps[5].delta.metric_values
```

Cy, linked to three of the four other members, has the highest centrality. A traversal's
sub-steps are steps too, so the order of the search can be read from their code:

```{python}
[sub.code for sub in club.steps[6].sub_steps]
```

The search starts at Ana, reaches Cy through Dee now that Ben has gone, and then reaches the two
newcomers from Cy. A step's `result` holds the value that the method returned, such as the visit
order of the search as node IDs, and `index` holds its position in the log, counted from 0, though
the printed lists number the steps from 1.

### Kinds of steps

The `kind` of a step places it in one of a few broad categories, which are useful for filtering:

| Kind | Recorded for |
|---|---|
| `"build_nodes"`, `"build_edges"` | `add_node()`, `add_nodes()`, `add_edge()`, `add_edges()`, and loading a dataset |
| `"generate"` | the generators, such as `add_path_graph()` or `add_grid_2d()` |
| `"remove"` | `delete_node()`, `delete_edge()`, `remove_selfloops()`, and other deletions |
| `"mutate"` | attribute updates, `relabel_nodes()`, and the `layout_*()` methods |
| `"metric"` | centrality measures and community detection that score or group the nodes |
| `"select"` | the `select_*`, `trav_*`, `deselect_*`, and `invert_*` methods and `clear_selection()` |
| `"traverse"` | `bfs()`, `dfs()`, and other traversals, with one sub-step per visited node |
| `"query"`, `"transform"` | queries and in-place transformations |
| `"annotate"` | a `note()` that no operation used, recorded as a step of its own |

Some analysis methods store their results with `set_node_attrs()` and are logged as the `"mutate"`
step of that call, under the name `set_node_attrs`, with the attribute that was written. A graph
loaded from a dataset, such as `karate_club()`, starts with a single step that adds all of its
nodes and edges at once. Methods that return a new graph, such as `k_core()` or `subgraph()`,
give the new graph a log of its own, which starts empty.

## Narrating with note()

`note()` holds a narration until the next operation that records a step, and that step then takes
the note instead of its automatic narration. Since `note()` returns the graph, it slots into a
method chain just before the step it describes, as in the book club example. Two details are worth
knowing. A note that no operation uses before the next `note()` call becomes a step of its own, of
kind `"annotate"`, so a sequence of notes can tell a story between operations. And a note still
pending when `play()` is called appears as a final annotation at the end of the replay:

```{python}
club.note("The club now meets monthly.").note("Who should organize the next meeting?")
club.steps[-1].kind, club.steps[-1].narration
```

The first note was flushed as an annotation step when the second was given, and the second stays
pending for the next operation, or for the end of a replay.

## Filtering and exporting

The `StepList` methods make it easy to pick out parts of a long log. `filter()` keeps the steps of
the given kinds or methods, each of which can be a single name or a list:

```{python}
club.steps.filter(kind=["build_nodes", "build_edges"])
```

`involves=` keeps the steps that touched any of the given nodes, by label, which traces the history
of a single node through a long session:

```{python}
club.steps.filter(involves="Eve")
```

Eve was added in step 3, linked in step 4, and visited in the traversal of step 7. `negate=True`
inverts any filter, so `filter(kind="select", negate=True)` drops the selection steps. Slicing a
`StepList`, and its `head()` and `tail()` methods, return `StepList` objects as well, so the methods
can be chained. `select()` extracts a few fields from each step as a list of dictionaries:

```{python}
club.steps.tail(3).select("method", "narration")
```

To keep the log alongside other results, `to_polars()` and `to_pandas()` convert it to a data
frame with one row per step, `to_dicts()` to a list of dictionaries, and `to_json()` to a JSON
string. The tables include the code, the narration, the nodes and edges added and removed, the
selections, the number of sub-steps, and a timestamp for each step:

```{python}
club.steps.to_polars().select("index", "kind", "method", "narration")
```

A table like this, written to a file next to the cleaned data, documents what was done to a network
before it was analyzed.

## Replaying with play()

`play()` turns the log into a *step player*: an animation of the graph, rebuilt step by step from
an empty graph, with the code and narration of each step below the drawing. For the book club:

```{python}
club.play()
```

The player opens on an empty graph. Each step then shows the graph as it was after that step, with
its changes highlighted: new nodes and edges glow green when they appear, removed ones are shown
faded in red, nodes whose attributes changed are outlined in amber, and selected ones are
highlighted. Nodes scored by an analysis are sized and colored by their scores, and the groups found
by community detection get a color each. A traversal is expanded into one frame per visited node,
which marks the current node, the nodes already visited, and the frontier of nodes about to be
reached. A last frame summarizes the finished graph.

The controls below the drawing step backward and forward, play and pause the animation, and set its
speed, and the slider jumps to any step. The player also responds to the keyboard: the arrow keys
step through the frames, the space bar plays and pauses, Home and End jump to the first and last
frames, and `L` shows a list of all the steps from which any one can be picked. Hovering over a
node shows its label and its state in the current frame.

### Options

`play()` shares many of its options with `plot()`: `layout=` chooses between `"force"`,
`"circular"`, and `"random"`, `theme=` between `"light"` and `"dark"`, and `width=`, `height=`,
`node_size=`, `edge_width=`, and `show_labels=` work as in [Static plots](22-plotting.qmd). The
canvas is 700 by 500 pixels by default. Three options are particular to the player:

- `auto_play=True` starts the animation as soon as the player is displayed
- `speed=` sets the initial speed, as a multiple of the default of about 1.2 seconds per step
- `layout_mode=` controls how the positions change from step to step

The default `layout_mode="progressive"` lays out the graph as it is at each step, starting from the
positions of the step before, and moves the nodes smoothly between frames, so the drawing grows
and reshapes as the graph does. `layout_mode="stable"` computes a single layout of every node that
ever appears, so nodes never move, which is easier to follow when the structure stays the same and
something else changes, as in a traversal. Graphs of more than 300 nodes always use the stable mode.

### Teaching an algorithm

The step log makes it easy to build an animation that explains an algorithm. The idea is to build
the graph, clear the log so that the construction is not part of the story, and then run the
algorithm. Comparing a breadth-first and a depth-first search on the same small graph:

```{python}
paths = ec.Graph().add_nodes(list("ABCDEFGH")).add_edges(
    [
        ("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("B", "E"),
        ("C", "F"), ("E", "G"), ("F", "G"), ("G", "H"),
    ]
)
paths.clear_steps()
paths.note("Breadth-first: finish each level before going deeper.").bfs(start="A")
paths.note("Depth-first: follow one path as far as it goes, then back up.").dfs(start="A")
paths.play(layout_mode="stable", speed=2.0)
```

`clear_steps()` empties the log but keeps the graph, and remembers which nodes and edges existed at
that point, so the replay shows them from the first frame instead of starting from an empty graph.
With the stable layout, the two searches run over the same picture: the breadth-first search spreads
out from A level by level, reaching B and C before any of their neighbors, while the depth-first
search visits D, backs up to follow the long path from B through E and G to F and C, and only then
backs up again to reach H. The sub-step code of each traversal confirms the two orders:

```{python}
[[sub.code for sub in step.sub_steps] for step in paths.steps]
```

### Replaying part of the log

For a long session, only part of the log may be worth replaying. There are two ways to choose the
steps, which differ in how the graph is rebuilt.

Calling `play()` on a filtered `StepList` replays only the chosen steps, but on top of the full
history: the graph at each frame includes everything done before, so a replay of the selection
steps shows the selections on the complete graph. `play(steps=)` instead rebuilds the graph from the
given steps alone, which suits a prefix of the log, such as the steps that built the club before
anyone left:

```{python}
club.play(steps=club.steps[:4], layout_mode="stable")
```

A subset passed to `steps=` that skips the steps creating some nodes doesn't show those nodes, so
for anything other than a prefix, filtering the `StepList` is usually the better choice:

```{python}
#| eval: false
club.steps.filter(kind="traverse").play()
```

### Saving a replay

Like the other step players, the result of `play()` is a `StepPlayer`, which displays itself in
notebooks and rendered documents. `output=` saves it as the replay is made, and the `save()` method
saves it afterwards. A path ending in `.html` writes the complete player, with its controls, to a
self-contained web page that can be shared or embedded, and any other extension writes the SVG of
the final frame:

```{python}
#| eval: false
paths.play(layout_mode="stable", output="bfs-vs-dfs.html")
```

## Managing the log

The log is part of the graph, so it lives as long as the graph does, and it grows with every
recorded operation. For most graphs this is negligible, but a long-running script that edits a graph
in a loop can accumulate many thousands of steps. `clear_steps()` resets the log at any point, for
example after the setup of an analysis, so that only the later steps are kept. It discards a pending
note as well, and it changes nothing about the graph itself:

```{python}
club.clear_steps()
len(club.steps), club.count_nodes()
```

The steps recorded after a reset are numbered from the beginning again.

## Summary

| Task | Method |
|---|---|
| See the log | `steps`, `print_steps()` |
| Narrate the next step | `note()` |
| Pick out steps | `steps.filter(kind=, method=, involves=, negate=)`, `head()`, `tail()`, slicing |
| Export the log | `steps.select()`, `to_dicts()`, `to_json()`, `to_polars()`, `to_pandas()` |
| Replay the log | `play()`, `steps.filter(...).play()`, `play(steps=)` |
| Save a replay | `play(output=)`, `save()` |
| Reset the log | `clear_steps()` |
